introduction: 'The site is down' describes a symptom, not a cause. A request can fail before it reaches your application, during TLS identity verification, or after the application receives it. This week gives each layer a distinct observation.

You will inspect one public documentation request and create a tiny local server with deliberate 200, 404 and 500 responses. All failure injection stays in the local lab or the client command; no global DNS or firewall changes are needed.
prerequisites: Finish week 1 and keep ~/dev-opps-lab. Stop the two week-1 servers with Ctrl+C.
Use Ubuntu Bash with Python 3, curl, dig and ip installed from the setup guide.
Public documentation inspection needs outbound HTTPS; the local fault lab works without internet.

concepts.title: Name, route, connection, identity, response
paragraphs: DNS maps a name to records, often IPv4 A or IPv6 AAAA addresses. Its time-to-live is how long a resolver may cache a record; it is not a guarantee that every client switches endpoints immediately. Your route table chooses how to reach an address. TCP then establishes a connection to a port.

For HTTPS over TCP, TLS verifies a server identity and encrypts the connection before HTTP carries a method, path, headers and body. A reverse proxy may terminate TLS and forward a request to an application. The application may need a database. Each boundary can fail independently.
concepts.example: A successful DNS lookup does not prove port 443 is reachable. A successful TLS handshake does not prove POST /tasks stores a task.
concepts.judgment: Start at the failing observation. Repeatedly restarting the app cannot repair a misspelled client hostname.

concepts.title: Addresses are relative to a network context
paragraphs: 127.0.0.1 is this network namespace's loopback interface. localhost is a name that commonly resolves to IPv4 and/or IPv6 loopback. 0.0.0.0 is a server bind wildcard for all IPv4 interfaces, not a useful remote destination.

An IPv4 /24 prefix fixes the first 24 bits. For example, 192.168.10.0/24 covers 256 addresses, including network and broadcast addresses in conventional subnet use. A default route matches destinations with no more-specific route. A container's loopback will later be different from the host's loopback.
concepts.example: A service listening only on a VM's 127.0.0.1 cannot be reached directly from your laptop using the VM's LAN address.
concepts.judgment: Inspect which interface listens before opening access. Wider binding and wider firewall access are separate changes.

concepts.title: An HTTP status is an application-layer observation
paragraphs: A 2xx status indicates the server reports success, 4xx describes a request it could not fulfill as submitted, and 5xx describes a server-side failure. The body still matters: a 200 with incorrect task content is not a correct system.

Connection refused usually means an active rejection, often no listener at that endpoint. A timeout means the operation did not finish within its deadline; dropped traffic, routing trouble or a slow service can all cause it. TLS verification failure means the identity/trust check failed. Do not turn verification off to declare recovery.
concepts.example: A 404 proves you received an HTTP response. A failed TCP connection cannot have an HTTP status from the intended app.
concepts.judgment: Use bounded timeouts so diagnostics finish. Do not treat a timeout as proof of one specific cause.

steps.title: Observe your network without changing it
steps.purpose: Use a normal Ubuntu terminal. The output describes this environment, which may be a WSL virtual network.

commands.code:
cd ~/dev-opps-lab
ip -brief address
ip route
dig docs.python.org A +noall +answer
dig docs.python.org AAAA +noall +answer
explain: ip -brief address shows interface names and addresses compactly. ip route prints the IPv4 route table without changing it.
dig asks the configured resolver for A then AAAA records. +noall suppresses other sections and +answer prints answers, including remaining TTLs.
commands.expected: Interfaces and routes appear. DNS may return aliases plus addresses; exact values and TTLs change.
commands.troubleshoot: If DNS is empty, run dig docs.python.org without output filters to inspect response status. Absence of AAAA alone does not imply A lookup failed.

steps.checkpoint: Identify loopback, one non-loopback interface, and whether a default route exists.

steps.title: Read a bounded HTTPS conversation
steps.purpose: Make one GET to public Python documentation. Do not add private authorization headers to verbose commands.

explain: --http1.1 chooses an easier-to-read HTTP/1.1 exchange. --verbose shows connection, TLS and request/response metadata on stderr.
--connect-timeout 5 bounds connection establishment; --max-time 15 bounds the whole operation. --output /dev/null discards only the response body.
The HTTPS URL supplies the hostname used for certificate verification. No insecure option is used.
commands.expected: A resolved address, a connection attempt, TLS verification information and an HTTP status. A redirect is possible and should be recorded rather than assumed absent.
commands.troubleshoot: A managed proxy can change the observed path; verbose output identifies proxy use. Record that boundary. Do not bypass certificate checks to force a green result.

steps.checkpoint: Write which output establishes DNS, connection, TLS and HTTP separately.

steps.title: Create a local server with explicit outcomes
steps.purpose: The short program below deliberately models three HTTP responses. It has no database or credentials and binds only loopback. Type it into the named file via the complete block.

commands.code:
cd ~/dev-opps-lab
cat > app/network_lab.py <<'PY'
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer

class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        responses = {'/': (200, b'healthy\n'), '/fail': (500, b'deliberate lab error\n')}
        status, body = responses.get(self.path, (404, b'not found\n'))
        self.send_response(status)
        self.send_header('Content-Type', 'text/plain')
        self.send_header('Content-Length', str(len(body)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(body)

ThreadingHTTPServer(('127.0.0.1', 8000), Handler).serve_forever()
PY
python3 app/network_lab.py
explain: cat with > writes this lab file. The quoted PY delimiter passes the enclosed Python text literally, without shell variable expansion.
BaseHTTPRequestHandler handles HTTP requests; do_GET runs for GET. A dictionary maps two paths; get supplies the 404 default.
send_response chooses the status. Headers identify type and byte length. end_headers ends the header section; wfile.write sends the body.
ThreadingHTTPServer listens on loopback port 8000 and serve_forever waits for requests. Run it in terminal A.
commands.expected: The server waits. It will log requests when terminal B sends them.
commands.troubleshoot: If the port is occupied, inspect it as taught in week 1 and stop only your previous lab server.

steps.checkpoint: Explain why /fail returns an intentional server error without crashing Python.

steps.title: Compare response failure with connection failure
steps.purpose: In terminal B, use exactly the same client observation for each path.

commands.code:
curl --include --max-time 3 http://127.0.0.1:8000/
curl --include --max-time 3 http://127.0.0.1:8000/absent
curl --include --max-time 3 http://127.0.0.1:8000/fail
curl --fail --show-error --max-time 3 http://127.0.0.1:8000/fail
printf 'exit status: %s\n' "$?"
explain: --include prints headers together with the body. --max-time bounds the request.
The first three commands inspect 200, 404 and 500. Without --fail, receiving a complete HTTP error response is normally still a successful curl transfer.
The fourth adds --fail so 500 returns nonzero; printf immediately captures that exit status.
commands.expected: 200/healthy, 404/not found, 500/deliberate lab error; the final failing transfer has status 22.
commands.troubleshoot: If every path returns a file listing, the old week-1 server is running instead. Compare process command lines.

steps.checkpoint: Draw client → name resolution → route/TCP → TLS (HTTPS only) → HTTP/proxy → application → database. Mark which parts your local lab actually contains.

failure.title: Point the client at the wrong port
failure.boundary: This changes only one client variable in terminal B. Confirm port 8001 has no listener before selecting it; do not stop an unrelated service.

explain: ss checks the intentionally wrong endpoint. LAB_URL is a shell variable used only by this command.
curl reports where it tried to connect and bounds the wait.
inject.expected: If 8001 is unused, curl reports connection failure before any HTTP response.
inject.troubleshoot: If ss lists a listener, choose another inspected unused local port and record it.

explain: ss identifies the real listener. A direct request to its observed port separates the service's health from the wrong client configuration.
investigate.troubleshoot: If it is absent, inspect terminal A before modifying the client again.

hints: Compare the port in LAB_URL with the local socket's port.
There is no TLS in this local HTTP request, so a certificate change cannot fix it.

explanation: The client was aimed at an endpoint with no listener. The application remained available at the correct endpoint. Repairing the client configuration is sufficient; restarting the healthy server adds no evidence.

explain: Reset the local client variable to the verified endpoint.
recover.expected: The variable changes without altering the host network.
recover.troubleshoot: Print the value with printf '%s\n' "$LAB_URL" if uncertain; it contains no secret.

explain: Repeat the request using the repaired variable.
verification.troubleshoot: A 404 means the connection works but the path is wrong; inspect the URL rather than the route.

questions.prompt: Why is successful name resolution insufficient evidence of availability?
questions.answer: It provides candidate addresses. Routing, transport acceptance, TLS identity and application behavior still need separate observations. A stale or correct DNS answer can point to an unavailable service.

questions.prompt: What does a 500 tell you that connection refused cannot?
questions.answer: A 500 is an HTTP response from some server in the path. Correlate proxy/application logs to identify which one. Connection refused happens before that HTTP exchange and does not establish that the app processed the request.

questions.prompt: curl works inside the server but fails on your laptop. What next?
questions.hint: Compare address scope and the two network paths.
questions.answer: Check the actual bind address, port and server interface, then routes and firewall/security-group rules from the laptop path. Loopback works only inside that network context. Do not immediately widen access to every source.

exercise.brief: Produce four diagnosis records: healthy HTTP, missing path, deliberate server error and wrong client port. Add an annotated network sketch for a future HTTPS Taskboard deployment.
constraints: No global DNS or firewall edits.
No requests to endpoints you do not control except the single public documentation observation.
deliverables: evidence/week-02.md with command, symptom, failing layer, disconfirming evidence and recovery.
A sketch marking where credentials and plaintext may exist.
acceptance: Each diagnosis names the earliest observed failing layer.
The sketch distinguishes the local HTTP lab from future TLS/proxy/database boundaries.
You can explain /24 and default route using your own example.
hints: Use identical timeouts so results are comparable.
solution: Capture each response with --include, then demonstrate the --fail exit status difference.
Use ss to rule out a missing application listener before investigating an HTTP path.
Mark TLS termination as a trust boundary, not just a decorative lock.

cleanup.code:
printf '%s\n' 'Press Ctrl+C in the terminal running app/network_lab.py.'
unset LAB_URL
cd ~/dev-opps-lab
git add app/network_lab.py
git commit -m 'Add a bounded network diagnosis lab'
explain: Stop the foreground lab server manually. unset removes the client variable from this shell.
cd selects the lab. git add stages only this program; commit records its intended outcomes.
cleanup.expected: The server stops and the diagnosis program is committed.
cleanup.troubleshoot: If Git says nothing to commit, inspect git status; do not manufacture a change just to get another commit.

references.title: curl options and exit codes
references.usedFor: Verbose request inspection, bounded timeouts and HTTP failure behavior.

references.title: Python HTTP handlers
references.usedFor: The small local handler's response lifecycle.

notes: The local program is a diagnostic teaching instrument. It does not implement production authentication, TLS or persistence.
